newsitem.title: IRAQ: Baghdad-backed Kurds attack rival faction.
newsitem.headline: Baghdad-backed Kurds attack rival faction.

text.p: Kurdish fighters of the Baghdad-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) attacked a rival militia on Friday in a bid to break out of the main northern Iraqi city of Arbil, witnesses said.
KDP fighters, firing Katyusha rockets and artillery shells, advanced to within two km (one mile) of the town of Koy Sanjak, held by the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), the witnesses said.
The KDP said it would halt its push once it had taken Koy Sanjak and given Arbil a breather from the PUK pressure.
"Today we want to enter Koy Sanjak, continue to Heibet Sultan mountain and then stop," local KDP commander Arif Tayfur told Reuters in the town of Degala, near the front line.
The PUK, led by Jalal Talabani, has closed on Arbil from several points, but it has advanced no closer than Degala, 30 km (20 miles) away to the south.
KDP leader Massoud Barzani on Thursday raised the stakes of a U.S. peace bid in northern Iraq by threatening to call for Baghdad's help in his struggle with the PUK.
Barzani, who allied himself with Iraqi forces in August and captured Arbil from the PUK, said he might ask President Saddam Hussein's army to come to his aid once more to curtail a PUK offensive.
The KDP strongman is due to meet Robert Pelletreau, U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs, in Turkey next week for talks on ending the Kurdish feud.
U.S. State Department officials met senior KDP figures in Washington on Thursday and urged the two factions to declare an immediate ceasefire.
U.S. officials also repeated warnings to Iraq and Iran to stay out of the conflict, saying any attempt by Baghdad to intervene militarily would be a "grave mistake".
The PUK and Iran deny allegations by the KDP and Iraq that Tehran is helping the PUK in its offensive to regain territory lost since late August.
Baghdad's intervention in August prompted the United States to fire cruise missiles at Iraqi military targets in southern Iraq and extend a no-fly zone in the south almost up to Baghdad.
U.S. defence officials said on Thursday they saw no sign of renewed Iraqi military movements as claimed by the PUK.
